lessons.osha-mission-construction:
**OSHA's Mission in Construction**

OSHA was created to help ensure safe and healthful working conditions for employees across all industries, including construction. In construction, this means helping prevent injuries and fatalities caused by falls, electrical hazards, struck-by incidents, trench collapses, equipment hazards, unsafe access, and other jobsite risks. Construction work is uniquely hazardous because conditions change from day to day — crews move from task to task, equipment arrives and departs, weather changes, and multiple trades often work side by side. OSHA uses standards, enforcement, training, outreach, education, and technical assistance to support workplace safety. OSHA's approach emphasizes prevention: identifying hazards early and controlling them before workers are hurt.

• OSHA's mission is to ensure safe and healthful working conditions for all employees.
• Construction is especially hazardous because site conditions change constantly.
• OSHA uses standards, enforcement, training, outreach, education, and assistance.
• Prevention — identifying and correcting hazards before incidents occur — is the goal.
lessons.part-1926-overview:
**Understanding 29 CFR Part 1926**

29 CFR Part 1926 contains OSHA's safety and health regulations for construction. It provides requirements for general safety and health provisions, personal protective equipment, fire protection, materials handling, hand and power tools, welding, electrical work, scaffolding, fall protection, cranes and hoisting, excavations, demolition, steel erection, concrete work, and many other construction-related topics. Part 1926 defines what must be inspected, guarded, protected, trained, and controlled on construction sites before work begins. A companion regulation, 29 CFR Part 1904, covers recording and reporting of work-related injuries and illnesses to help employers identify and correct hazards.

• 29 CFR Part 1926 is the primary OSHA standard for construction safety and health.
• It covers fall protection, scaffolds, excavations, electrical safety, cranes, PPE, and more.
• Part 1926 defines jobsite safety requirements before and during construction activities.
• 29 CFR Part 1904 covers required injury and illness recordkeeping for construction employers.
lessons.focus-four-hazards:
**The Construction Focus Four Hazards**

OSHA's Construction Focus Four training addresses the four major hazard categories most strongly associated with serious injuries and fatalities on construction sites. Falls occur when workers are exposed to unprotected edges, floor openings, roofs, or elevated surfaces. Struck-by hazards involve workers being hit by moving vehicles, swinging equipment, flying objects, or falling materials. Caught-in or between hazards occur when workers are caught in, compressed by, or crushed between equipment, materials, or structures. Electrical hazards arise from contact with energized wiring, tools, equipment, or overhead power lines. Recognizing these four groups is the starting point for preventing the most serious construction injuries.

• The Focus Four hazards account for a large proportion of serious construction injuries and fatalities.
• Falls: unprotected edges, roofs, floor openings, and elevated work surfaces.
• Struck-by: moving vehicles, swinging equipment, falling tools and materials.
• Caught-in/between: crushed by equipment or between structures; electrical: energized contact.
lessons.employee-rights-construction:
**Employee Rights on Construction Sites**

Under OSHA, construction workers have the right to a safe and healthful workplace, to receive training about the hazards they face, to review relevant safety records, and to raise safety and health concerns without being punished, threatened, or treated unfairly. This protection from retaliation is essential in construction because workers are often the first to notice changing jobsite conditions. Employees have the right to request an OSHA inspection, to speak with OSHA inspectors, and to be informed about OSHA citations issued to their employer. Workers can also request information about chemicals and hazardous materials through safety data sheets and the hazard communication standard.

• Workers have the right to a safe workplace, training, and access to safety records.
• Employees may report unsafe conditions without fear of retaliation.
• Workers can request an OSHA inspection and speak with OSHA inspectors.
• Construction workers are often closest to changing jobsite hazards — their voice matters.
lessons.employer-responsibilities-construction:
**Employer and Supervisor Responsibilities**

Employers on construction sites are responsible for providing a workplace free from serious recognized hazards, complying with applicable OSHA standards, examining workplace conditions, providing required training before employees are exposed to hazards, and maintaining required injury and illness records. Employers must plan work safely, coordinate safety responsibilities with subcontractors, provide the correct PPE and protective systems, inspect equipment and work areas regularly, and correct unsafe conditions promptly. OSHA standards for certain construction activities require a designated competent person — someone capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards and authorized to take corrective action. Examples include daily inspection of excavations and evaluation of scaffolding before use.

• Employers must provide a construction site free from serious recognized hazards.
• Training and PPE must be provided before employees are exposed to hazards.
• Competent persons are required by OSHA for certain activities such as excavation inspections.
• Employers must correct hazards promptly and coordinate safety across all trades.
lessons.osha-inspections-enforcement:
**OSHA Inspections, Enforcement, and Correction**

OSHA may inspect construction sites in response to worker complaints, referrals, serious incidents, fatalities, catastrophic events, targeted program criteria, or follow-up from prior inspections. Inspections may be announced or unannounced. If OSHA identifies violations, the employer may receive citations requiring correction within set timeframes. Serious violations carry civil penalties. Willful or repeat violations carry higher penalties. The goal of enforcement is to drive hazard correction and strengthen worker protection. The best approach for any employer is to identify and correct hazards before an inspection occurs — proactive hazard control prevents injuries and avoids citations.

• OSHA may inspect construction sites after complaints, incidents, fatalities, or through targeted programs.
• Violations can result in citations requiring hazard correction within set timeframes.
• Serious, willful, and repeat violations carry progressively higher civil penalties.
• Proactive hazard correction before an inspection protects workers and avoids citations.
lessons.recordkeeping-near-misses-construction:
**Recordkeeping, Reporting, and Near Misses**

Under 29 CFR Part 1904, most employers with more than 10 employees must record work-related injuries and illnesses on the OSHA 300 Log, 301 Incident Report, and 300A Annual Summary. Certain severe injuries and all work-related fatalities must also be reported to OSHA within specified timeframes. Beyond compliance, these records are prevention tools. Reviewing injury trends can reveal patterns in task types, equipment, or work areas that point to hazards needing correction. Near misses — events where injury almost occurred but did not — are equally important. A dropped tool that narrowly missed a worker below, a trench wall shift, or a trip over debris without injury are all signals that a hazard exists and should be corrected before the next event causes harm.

• 29 CFR Part 1904 requires most employers to maintain OSHA 300, 301, and 300A records.
• Fatalities and certain severe injuries must be reported to OSHA within required timeframes.
• Injury and illness records help identify hazard patterns and drive corrective action.
• Near misses are warning signs — they must be reported and investigated to prevent future injuries.
